rationale: A wins because it has the sharper editor brain: it knows the story is in the missing denominator, not the milestone confetti. "Whatnot says it hit $3B in live-auction sales. It won't say what sellers actually make" is the cleanest press angle in either set. But A nearly steps on a rake with "worth less than one times revenue it doesn't keep," while B's "sneakers and laptops" and "sneakers and phones" invent specificity the update did not give it.
gaps_in_A: "worth less than one times revenue it doesn't keep" is bad math and bad wording. A near-$5B valuation against $3B GMV is not less than one times anything obvious.
"the shutdown-and-retreat cycle of Western live-shopping efforts" may be true market context, but it is not in the supplied update and needs sourcing before it becomes a pitch premise.
"who loses if the number is real" pushes the competitor-threat frame harder than the facts allow; the update says expansion, not incumbent damage.
gaps_in_B: "sneakers and laptops" and "sneakers and phones" are invented examples. The update says fashion and electronics, not those products.
"Trading-card sellers built Whatnot's business" overstates the supplied fact. The update says Whatnot started with trading cards and collectibles; it does not prove those sellers built the business.
"any prior seller complaints about payout terms" reaches for a controversy not in the update. Fine as reporting to investigate, sloppy as proof the founder can offer.
"Next step: journalist-fit-check" is premature. The founder needs take-rate, seller payout, category-level, and Asia-versus-US evidence before matching this to reporters.
